articles.body:
More Americans see domestic terrorist attacks as a larger threat than foreign ones, according to a new poll.

In the Reuters/Ipsos poll , 33 percent of respondents said domestic terrorism is the most significant threat to the average American’s safety, while 20 percent said the same of foreign terrorism. Forty-two percent identified random violent acts, like mass shootings, as the largest threat.

The poll also asked respondents whether foreign or domestic extremist ideologies pose a greater risk, with 61 percent choosing homegrown extremism and 34 percent pointing abroad.

The survey’s results arrive only a few weeks before the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, which were perpetrated by foreign terrorist organizations. The attacks had a major effect on American security and foreign policy in the following decades and led to several U.S. wars and conflicts in the Middle East.

In recent years, there have been multiple notable incidents of political violence in the U.S. carried out by Americans, including the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol; the multiple attempts on President Trump’s life; and the killings of former Minnesota state House Speaker Melissa Hortman (D) and conservative commentator Charlie Kirk.

In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio convened officials from more than 60 countries to raise awareness about what his department warned was a rise in far-left political violence around the world.

The secretary pressed for an “international response” to the issue at the summit, which marked a widening of President Trump’s focus on addressing left-leaning political violence as what his administration considers the most important terrorist threat facing the U.S.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll took place from Aug. 28 to 31, featuring 1,167 people and 3 percentage points as its margin of error.

articles.title: US Pursues Deportees Abroad for Hundreds of Millions in Unpaid Fines
articles.summary: The Trump administration is hiring private contractors to track down deported migrants who it claims owe the US government hundreds of millions of dollars in...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The Trump administration is hiring private contractors to track down deported migrants who it claims owe the US government hundreds of millions of dollars in unpaid penalties, a move that will test how far its immigration crackdown can reach across borders.

US Customs and Border Protection says it is trying to recover about $423 million in fines and fees from more than 66,300 people who have been removed from the US. Last month, the agency agreed to pay as much as $36 million to four firms to find people in Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala it claims are in arrears, according to a notice posted on a government procurement website.

The initiative marks a striking expansion of President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts that would extend the government's power over people it has already expelled from the US. However, collecting could be challenging. It's unclear whether the US can legally require people who have been removed from the country to pay. The contract notice doesn't explain how the US could compel payments or what role, if any, the governments of Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala would have.

It's also far from certain whether deportees would be able to pay what the US says they owe. Many may have limited resources or lack access to a US bank account, which is required to pay the fines, according to payment methods described in federal documents. In past cases, the US has threatened that unpaid fines could affect future immigration cases.

The contractors may photograph homes or obtain utility bills, employment records or court papers to locate deportees and establish their ability to pay, according to the contract documents.

CBP awarded the two-year contracts last month to Global Recovery Group, The Baptiste Group, Caduceus Inc. and Response AI Solutions, according to federal records. Each agreement has a maximum value of $9 million. The companies didn't respond to requests for comment.

The amount CBP is trying to collect represents only a small portion of the larger pool of penalties imposed by the US Department of Homeland Security. From Trump's return to office on Jan. 20, 2025, through July 16, 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, DHS's enforcement arm, issued more than 103,000 civil fines totaling more than $84 billion, according to DHS. By July 16, the government had collected just $1.2 million.

articles.title: Serbia and Uzbekistan strike strategic partnership in Mirziyoyev's first Belgrade visit
articles.summary: Uzbek President Mirziyoyev's first official visit to Belgrade produced 20 signed agreements on transport, energy, digitalisation, and labour mobility, alongs...
articles.body:
Uzbekistan and Serbia signed a strategic partnership declaration in Belgrade on Tuesday, with the two countries' presidents agreeing 20 bilateral agreements covering trade, transport, energy, digitalisation and labour mobility during Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev's first official visit to Serbia.

Mirziyoyev and his Serbian counterpart Aleksandar Vučić held talks before attending a business forum that brought together more than 200 government and business representatives from both countries, where they signed further commercial agreements.

"Serbia and Uzbekistan are two countries separated by thousands of kilometres, yet they are close in spirit, sharing a deep appreciation for hospitality, honour and mutual respect. Today, they are writing a new chapter in their shared history," Vučić said.

Mirziyoyev called the decision to establish a strategic partnership historic.

"Today, we made a historic decision to establish a strategic partnership between Serbia and Uzbekistan. Once again, this shows that this is a historic visit and that we have made a historic decision," Mirziyoyev said.

Bilateral trade reached a record $41.9 million last year, up 27% from $32.9 million in 2024, according to the Serbian Chamber of Commerce.

Serbian exports of agricultural and food products to Uzbekistan rose 54.1% in the first seven months of 2026.

The two governments are now preparing negotiations on a bilateral free trade agreement, with a working group established for that purpose.

The 20 documents signed cover international road and rail transport, agriculture and water management, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, tourism, culture, IT and digitalisation, labour migration, occupational health, environmental protection, cinema and joint film production, and support for people with disabilities.

Vučić said a direct air link between Belgrade and Tashkent could be operational within seven to eight months.

The countries also agreed on an industrial cooperation action plan for 2026-2028.

With transport connectivity a major priority for both countries, Serbia and Uzbekistan signed documents in support of the Middle Corridor, the trans-Caspian trade route linking Central Asia to Europe through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey.

The corridor has gained strategic importance since Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted the northern overland route through Russian territory.

Vučić awarded Mirziyoyev Serbia's highest state decoration, the Order of the Republic of Serbia on a Grand Collar, and the two presidents attended a ceremony naming a Belgrade street after Tashkent.

articles.title: There’s a simple way the Fed could help calm the bond market
articles.summary: Investors are increasingly worried about government deficits and persistent inflation, driving up the price of money. The Federal Reserve can ease some of th...
articles.body:
Investors are increasingly worried about government deficits and persistent inflation, driving up the price of money. The Federal Reserve can ease some of those nerves.

The conflict in the Middle East intensified last week, pushing up energy prices again and forcing heavily indebted countries to borrow more to increase defense spending and fund the war. That deepened a global rout in the bond market, sending yields to multi-year and multi-decade highs . Higher yields raise borrowing costs for consumers for everything from mortgages and credit cards to the US government's $40 trillion debt.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has been mostly silent on where he believes interest rates could be heading. However, in a major speech last month at an economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Warsh gave markets a hint , saying there was more "work to do" in fighting inflation — a signal that rate hikes could be around the corner.

Investors welcomed Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, underscoring how keen they are to get more clarity on his economic views. Fiscal concerns and a flood of corporate borrowing to fund the AI build-out are the biggest drivers of the surge in yields. But greater transparency from Warsh could be an important source of stability for the bond market — and a much better alternative to the central bank deploying its massive $6.7 trillion balance sheet to control yields, as it did during the Great Recession and World War II.

"The Fed's responsibility is confined to just controlling inflation and if Warsh can just explain policy better in the next few months, then that source of anxiety is likely to ease," Derek Tang, a policy economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, told CNN. "But the Fed does have firepower with its unlimited balance sheet."

US Treasury yields ticked slightly higher on Tuesday as traders monitored oil prices and geared up for inflation data set to be released later this week. After surging last week, yields were steadier this week. The 10-year yield traded at 4.79%, near its highest level since 2025 and on the cusp of its highest level since 2023.

Warsh has said repeatedly that the Fed is committed to its 2% annual inflation target. But that hasn't been enough to reassure bond investors.

Shortly after Warsh held a news conference following the Fed's July monetary policy meeting, long-term bond yields surged. That was likely a reflection of doubts about the Fed chairman's commitment to taming inflation, an adjustment period to a quieter Fed , or simply expectations for future rate hikes.

articles.title: Western Michigan appealing last-second Hail Mary loss to Michigan
articles.summary: The Mid-American Conference (MAC) formally asked the NCAA to overturn the result of Saturday’s Michigan vs. Western Michigan football game, which ended on a last-second Hail Mary touchdown pass, handing the Wolverines a victory after the officials put a second back on the clock. In a statement on Tuesday, MAC commissioner Jon Steinbrecher said it…
articles.body:
The Mid-American Conference (MAC) formally asked the NCAA to overturn the result of Saturday’s Michigan vs. Western Michigan football game, which ended on a last-second Hail Mary touchdown pass, handing the Wolverines a victory after the officials put a second back on the clock.

In a statement on Tuesday, MAC commissioner Jon Steinbrecher said it was clear to him “replay protocol was not properly followed in determining whether time remained on the game clock.”

“The established replay protocol requires that the game clock displayed on the program feed be used in determining whether time remained. Instead, the Big Ten Conference replay crew relied upon the clock feed embedded within its replay system,” Steinbrecher said. “As a result, one second was placed back on the game clock and an additional play was awarded.”

Saturday’s game appeared finished after Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood heaved a last-second throw to the back of the end zone, which fell incomplete as time expired with Western Michigan winning 12-7.

However, the Big Ten officiating crew in Ann Arbor determined a Western Michigan defensive player touched the ball while out of bounds with one second remaining.

The officials put a second back on the clock, and Michigan pulled off a stunning Hail Mary to win 13-12.

“As a result, the Mid-American Conference has submitted formal appeals to the NCAA FBS Oversight Committee and the College Football Playoff,” Steinbrecher said.

The conference requested that those bodies recognize Western Michigan “as the actual winner of the game for purposes of their respective rankings, evaluations and selection deliberations, and take such other corrective action as may be within their authority.”

Such a request is extremely rare, and The Hill has reached out to the NCAA for comment.

Michigan fell out of the AP Top 25 poll this week following the narrow victory against its in-state foe. The Wolverines were ranked 16th in the poll to open the season.

articles.title: Bessent’s ‘Fever’-Quelling Debt Buybacks Put Wall Street on Edge
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is set to reveal how far he’s initially willing to go restrain US bond yields via an expanded buyback program that has Wall...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is set to reveal how far he's initially willing to go restrain US bond yields via an expanded buyback program that has Wall Street dealers on edge.

The Treasury Department is expected to announce on Wednesday the size of the next day's operation to repurchase outstanding 10-year to 20-year securities; past precedent indicates it would be at 11 a.m. in Washington. It will be the first such release since the Treasury shocked market participants Aug. 19 by saying it would "at least double" the $2 billion sizes it had penciled in just two weeks before.

Bessent has repeatedly declined to tip how big the Sept. 10 buyback will be, though his public remarks have helped fan expectations among many that it will exceed $4 billion. On Tuesday, he characterized the initiative as aimed at cooling "this fever that was building" in the market, in an apparent reference to a selloff that last month sent longer-dated yields to the highest in years.

With 10-year yields, which are key for US mortgage rates, now even higher than last month's levels, stakes are high. Coming in at just $4 billion could prove a disappointment to investors, adding to selling pressure in the world's biggest bond market.

But opting for a giant total — Morgan Stanley calculates $10 billion as a practical cap — could set a new baseline for subsequent longer-dated buybacks, with the next one due in two weeks. It could also suggest Bessent's angst about yield levels has deepened further since last month's surprise move.

A larger increase "would be an admission that the Treasury hadn't thought through its hasty August 19 announcement in the first place," Lou Crandall, a senior economist at Wrightson ICAP, wrote in a note to clients.

Crandall sees something in the $5 to $6 billion range as a plausible starting point, while acknowledging even larger increases wouldn't be out of character given the rapid shifts in the Treasury's strategy during the past few weeks.

Amplifying the immediate consequences of Wednesday's news: it's due to come just hours before the department's next sale of 10-year notes, and a day before a 30-year bond auction.

The Treasury declined to respond to a request for comment on its upcoming announcement.

The study, published in the Journal of Business Research, looked at how digital shopping carts were associated with spending and shopping behavior. Researchers studied smart shopping carts at a well-known German supermarket chain during March 2025. They analyzed 12,418 individual shopping sessions over the month. Of those trips, 9,422 involved shoppers actively using the smart-cart technology. These were grocery carts fitted with tablet-style screens on the handle. Shoppers could use the technology for digital shopping lists, personalized recommendations and in-store navigation. The carts also supported checkout-free payment. Researchers recorded how much shoppers spent and how many items they bought. They also measured how long each shopping trip lasted. The differences were substantial. Smart-cart shoppers spent 32% more on average than non-users. They also purchased 25% more items and spent 23% more time in the store. The spending gap grew during afternoons and weekends. Meanwhile, shoppers tended to spend the most time in stores during the evening. Why retailers may love smart shopping carts Those numbers naturally caught the researchers' attention because a cart that increases shopper engagement could become a valuable tool for stores. Dr. Sabrina Gottschalk, a lecturer in marketing at Bayes Business School and lead author of the study, said the findings suggest retailers could see significant revenue gains from the technology. She pointed to special offers and new product recommendations as potential opportunities. The screen also creates another place for retailers and brands to advertise while someone is actively deciding what to buy. That last part catches my attention. The screen may help you find something faster. At the same time, it can put another product in front of you when you are already in shopping mode. Your grocery cart has essentially become another screen competing for your attention. Did the AI shopping cart actually make people spend more? There is an important limitation here. The study found an association between smart-cart use and higher spending. Because the researchers observed shopping behavior rather than randomly assigning shoppers to different carts, the results do not prove that the technology itself caused the 32% increase. Someone choosing a smart cart may already have planned a bigger grocery run. A shopper with a longer list could also be more interested in technology designed to make navigating the store easier. Then researchers found another wrinkle. They looked at shoppers who interacted with the smart-cart screen more than 20 times during a single trip. These "superusers" bought significantly more items and stayed in the store longer. However, they did not spend more money overall. Once screen interaction reached higher levels, spending and basket size eventually began to decline. Researchers suggested that some of these shoppers may have been using the technology more for the experience than because they wanted to buy more. So the research does not prove that tapping a smart-cart screen automatically sends your grocery bill soaring. Still, a 32% difference in average spending is hard to ignore. BABY BOOMERS HATE 10 THINGS ABOUT TODAY'S GROCERY STORES AI shopping carts are already spreading across the U.S. While this particular study happened in Germany, smart carts are already rolling through grocery stores here in the U.S. Instacart says thousands of its AI-powered Caper Carts are deployed across more than 100 cities. The company also said in May 2026 that Caper Carts spanned 15 states and were available across more than a dozen retail banners overall. U.S. retailers using the technology include Kroger and Schnucks, along with Wakefern banners such as ShopRite and Fairway Market. Weis Markets has also begun deploying them at select stores. Caper Carts use cameras, built-in scales and other sensors to understand what shoppers put into or remove from their baskets. The screen can also deliver recommendations while customers move through the store. Amazon has a competing version called Dash Cart. Its newest Dash Cart displays prices and keeps a running total as you shop. It can offer personalized nearby deals, help navigate the store and let shoppers bypass the traditional checkout line. Amazon says the newest version will expand to dozens of additional Whole Foods Market locations across the U.S. by the end of 2026. That means this technology could become a much more familiar part of your grocery run. Your grocery cart can become an advertising screen Here is where I think smart carts become especially interesting. A traditional shopping cart holds your groceries. A smart cart can also put promotions directly in front of you while you move around the store. Instacart says its Caper Cart technology can use signals such as what is already in your basket and where the cart is inside the store to decide when to surface recommendations. The company says prompts designed to remind shoppers about forgotten items have increased average basket size in its own testing. Think about how powerful that can be. You turn down an aisle and a promotion appears for something nearby. Something already in your cart could also lead to a recommendation for another product. Sometimes that could save you money or remind you about something you genuinely need. Other times, you may end up buying something that never appeared on your shopping list. Retailers have spent decades figuring out where to position products. Smart carts bring another version of that strategy directly onto a screen that moves through the store with you. What your smart shopping cart may learn about you There is also a data side to these carts that deserves attention. Instacart says its Caper Carts use basket-facing camera sensors and outward-facing cameras. They also rely on built-in scales and location-tracking systems. The company says those systems can detect which products enter or leave the basket and how shoppers move through store aisles. Instacart also says its technology can connect physical shopping interactions with purchase history. That data can make the cart more useful. It can also help make recommendations more targeted. That is why I would pay attention to the privacy settings connected to any grocery-store account or loyalty program you use. Take a look at what information the retailer collects and what controls it gives you over personalized advertising. MARYLAND MOVES TO BAN SURVEILLANCE PRICING IN GROCERY STORES How to keep a smart cart from increasing your grocery bill You do not have to avoid an AI shopping cart simply because there is a screen attached to it. Some of the technology can genuinely make grocery shopping easier. The key is using those features without letting every recommendation change what you planned to buy. 1) Start with a shopping list Decide what you need before you enter the store. When the cart suggests something extra, compare it with the list you already made. 2) Watch your running total This could actually be one of the best features of a smart cart. Keep an eye on your total as you shop instead of waiting for the final surprise at checkout. 3) Treat recommendations like advertising A recommendation may be useful, but remember why it appeared on your screen. The retailer benefits when another product lands in your cart. 4) Check the actual price Do not assume a coupon or promoted product gives you the best deal. Compare prices and look at the unit price when package sizes differ. 5) Compare your receipts Here is a simple experiment you can do yourself. Compare what you spend during a few smart-cart trips with your regular grocery runs. You may discover the technology helps you stay organized. You could also find that those convenient suggestions are adding more to your bill than you realized. For more ways to cut grocery costs, check out our article on 8 apps that can cut your food bill. Kurt's key takeaways I like technology that removes some of the aggravation from grocery shopping. Seeing your running total can be useful. Getting out of the store without standing in a long checkout line sounds pretty appealing to me too. What I want you to remember is that the screen on your cart has another purpose. Retailers can use it to put offers and recommendations in front of you at exactly the moment you are deciding what to buy. That does not make every suggestion a bad deal. Some could genuinely save you money. Still, the 32% spending difference in this study caught my attention. As these carts become more common in grocery stores, I think we should pay as much attention to how they influence our shopping as we do to how much time they save us. Enjoy the convenience and take the discounts when they really help. Most of all, keep your shopping list and your budget in charge. Would you grab an AI-powered shopping cart if it helped you skip the checkout line, or would knowing smart-cart users spent 32% more make you stick with a regular cart? articles.title: Veterans group launches new campaign against Trump’s planned arch
articles.summary: VoteVets, the largest Democratic veterans group in the U.S., on Tuesday launched a new messaging campaign against President Trump’s planned arch across from Arlington National Cemetery. Paul Eaton, a retired major general and VoteVets adviser, argued in a video posted to social media that the project is “entirely inappropriate and borders on sacrilege to the…
articles.body:
VoteVets, the largest Democratic veterans group in the U.S., on Tuesday launched a new messaging campaign against President Trump’s planned arch across from Arlington National Cemetery.

Paul Eaton, a retired major general and VoteVets adviser, argued in a video posted to social media that the project is “entirely inappropriate and borders on sacrilege to the men and women buried” there to break the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and the cemetery with the 250-foot arch.

“The U.S. Park Service says that construction for this arch will be 20 hours a day for up to three years. Every weekday somebody is buried at Arlington National Cemetery,” Eaton said, pointing to the potential disruption of such solemn ceremonies.

The video also featured Karen Meredith, a Gold Star mother whose son is buried at Arlington, who argued a planned observation deck on the arch for tourists to look out over the city and cemetery would disrupt the quiet solitude of the hallowed ground.

“We don’t need tourists overlooking funerals. I’m just appalled,” Meredith said. “We need everybody to speak out about this.”

The campaign, which is also supported by political advocacy group Home of the Brave, comes as the administration has imminent plans to break ground on the arch. The National Park Service recently backed its proposed Memorial Circle location across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial — even after it found the monument would have “ adverse effects ” on several historic sites as well as the skyline of the nation’s capital.

Eaton pressed for veterans to reach out to their lawmakers and the National Capital Planning Commission to voice their opposition to the arch, on which the administration suggested it would begin construction this month.

“We are pleased to announce that after a very long wait (over 125 years!), we are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on social media Thursday.

Hoping to halt the planned project, several groups have brought lawsuits against the administration, including Vietnam War veterans , who are seeking an emergency court order to block the administration from breaking ground.

articles.title: How Canada decided to hurt its own economy, raise its inflation—and most Canadians approved because they’re so angry at Trump
articles.summary: Oxford economists predict Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s retaliatory tariffs will slow economic growth and raise consumer prices.
articles.body:
Economists are warning that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's " dollar-for-dollar " tariff strategy could mean some economic pain for the Great White North, but Canadians are so frustrated with the Trump administration they support the move anyway.

Canada implemented retaliatory tariffs of 15% to 50% that took effect on Tuesday and will impact hundreds of U.S. goods, including paper, steel, aluminum, furniture, as well as cheese and seafood. The levies were in response to a breakdown of trade talks between the countries and the Trump administration's piling on of tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods earlier this summer.

But the strategy of imposing steep import taxes on the U.S. could cause a phenomenon similar to what happened to American importers, where Canadians carry the burden of the tariffs. In a report published after Canada announced the tariffs on Aug. 25, Oxford Economics analysts warned that while the retaliatory tariffs may help protect some domestic manufacturers, it will also force Canadian businesses to absorb added business costs and increase consumer prices.

Canada depends on the U.S. buyers for about 70% of its exports, and the U.S. economy is about 13-times larger than Canada's.

Oxford projected that Canada's GDP will likely grow by 0.8% in 2026, but tariffs will reduce growth in 2027 by 0.2% to 0.3% relative to its August baseline calculations. It predicted inflation to increase by about 0.3% compared to the August 2027 baseline.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs will most likely be felt in certain regions of the country, Oxford economists said. For example, Ontario, New Brunswick , and Quebec have the highest concentration of manufacturers impacted by the tariffs and rely the most on U.S. exports. British Columbia meanwhile has the highest percentage of its exports, 6.1%, subject to Section 338 Trump invoked to tax Canadian exports. Alberta, Newfoundland, and Saskatchewan—provinces that produce the most oil—will be less impacted on average.

"Canada's new retaliatory tariffs will help some industries but hurt most and weaken economic growth across the country by raising costs for producers and consumers," economists Tony Stillo and Michael Davenport wrote. "The macroeconomic impacts on Canada will likely be modest, but the regional and sectoral implications will be far more significant."

What are the stakes for Canada in its trade war with the U.S.?

Even as the economic stakes of Canada's involvement in the trade war escalates, Canadians have supported Carney, who is one of the few world leaders standing up to Trump, in the hopes that the import taxes on the U.S. will mount economic pressure and protect Canadian industry.

articles.body:
The U.S. military destroyed five Iranian oil tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Tuesday in response to attempted Iranian missile launches at U.S. Navy warships, the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) announced.

The U.S. forces disabled IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1 and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, along with M/T Derya near Kharg Island, an island located in the northern Persian Gulf.

The U.S. military directed the crews on vessels to abandon ships before firing at the tankers, according to Centcom. No U.S. personnel were harmed in the attacks.

“Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies,” Centcom said in a statement. “Iran has no means by which to defend these vessels.”

U.S. strikes on Tuesday came a day after Iran launched attacks against Navy ships that Centcom has not publicly acknowledged, The Wall Street Journal reported. No ships were hit in the attack.

Fox News was the first outlet to report on the Tuesday U.S. attacks.

On Saturday, the U.S. military “ permanently disabled ” three IRGC crude oil tankers near Kharg Island and in the Gulf of Oman, retaliating for Iran’s strikes against U.S. Navy vessels.

A day later, the IRGC attacked a remotely operated U.S. military vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media.

The flare-ups in the Middle East come as Brent crude, an international standard for oil, was trading at $97 per barrel Tuesday.

Iran will announce a “restricted zone” near the Strait of Hormuz, and all ships that come into the zone and do not cooperate with Iran will be placed on a sanctions list, Press TV, an Iranian state media outlet, reported on Sunday .

Meanwhile, the U.S. military has continued to enforce the naval blockade in the Arabian Sea. U.S. forces have redirected 94 commercial ships, disabled three and boarded another to ensure compliance since mid-July, Centcom said in an update Monday.

articles.title: Bessent: We can grow our way out of debt with 3% GDP growth
articles.summary: "We don't have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem," Scott Bessent said during a Q&A in Dallas on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that he believes the US can grow its way out of debt if it can achieve annual economic growth of 3%.

"We don't have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem," Bessent said during a Q&A at SMU Cox School of Business in Dallas. He said if the US tries to contain spending coupled with 3% growth, "we [can] grow our way out of this."

The total US national debt recently surpassed $40 trillion , and the annual fiscal deficit is projected to top $2 trillion by the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30.

"We'll get to the other side of this Iran conflict and the underlying economy is very, very strong, and I think reaccelerating," he added, pointing to how incentives in the big tax law passed last year are leading to new construction of manufacturing plants, pointing to Pepsi ( PEP ) expanding a Frito-Lay plant in Arizona, Winnebago ( WGO ) buying a battery plant, and Boeing ( BA ) increasing capacity of its Dreamliner.

On the spending side, Bessent said he's been working with the director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russ Vought, on a fiscal consolidation plan to bring the deficit down. He noted he would prefer not to rush it through a lame-duck Congress if Democrats take back one or both houses of Congress in the upcoming midterms.

He also said that if not for the Supreme Court striking down President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, the US would have been collecting $180 billion to pay down the deficit.

Bessent also pointed again in the interim to buying back long-term Treasury bonds .

"Interest rates are high, but … we're going to do more bond buybacks, which is just taking the most liquid portion of the bond market, liquefying it, and giving the bond buyers money to buy more," Bessent said.

Current interest rates, he said, are the most correlated that they've been with energy prices, and he thinks that will break. In a year or two, he said, the market will be oversupplied with oil, given the energy relationship the US is building with Venezuela now and as things normalize in the Middle East.

President Trump’s foreign policy approach in the second term – hard border security, shifting weapons support to allied-financed purchases, hawkish actions in the Middle East and reforming foreign assistance – will yield over $320 billion in net taxpayer savings over four years, according to a new report from a GOP-linked group.

The Trump administration invested around $186 billion to restore “deterrence,” including military operations abroad and strong border enforcement – yielding approximately $326 billion in net taxpayer savings over the president’s four-year term or nearly $2,500 per American household, the report said. With the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), the joint U.S. and NATO procurement mechanism to fund and supply Ukraine with U.S.-made weapons, the administration is projected to save taxpayers $258 billion . By eliminating mass parole and lowering the number of illegal immigrants in the U.S. as part of its effort to seal off the U.S.-Mexico border , the administration averted about $158 billion in projected taxpayer costs, according to the analysis. The administration has also largely dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) , while some of its functions have been transferred to the State Department. articles.title: 'Flat-rate' COLA cuts Social Security for most Americans, critics say
articles.summary: A proposal to change Social Security COLAs aims to help low earners but critics warn it would cut benefits for most.
articles.body:
An old idea to increase all Social Security recipients' benefits by the same dollar amount each year is gaining traction, but some say this would be a disaster for middle-income Americans.

In 1987, former Democratic Rep. Tim Penny from Minnesota's 1st Congressional District proposed a " Flat-Rate COLA " that would pay all beneficiaries the same cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA. The COLA dollar amount would be set at the COLA received by a beneficiary at the 20th percentile. By doing this, lowest-income beneficiaries would receive larger benefits, poverty would be reduced, and Social Security's insolvency would be delayed, advocates said.

The trust fund that supplements incoming payroll taxes to pay monthly Social Security benefits is expected to run dry by the end of 2032, according to the program's trustees . When that happens, law requires benefits to be reduced by an estimated 22% to ensure the program's costs do not exceed its revenues.

But critics of the flat-rate COLA , like the nonprofit and nonpartisan AARP, calculate that 80% of beneficiaries would see the purchasing power of their benefits erode year after year, leaving many in or near poverty.

"For 80% of beneficiaries, the flat-rate COLA would erode the inflation protection that Social Security has always provided, and the impact would grow as people age," said AARP, which serves 125 million Americans age 50-plus and their families, in a blog . "Because the impact of COLA cuts multiplies over time, a flat-rate COLA would intensify financial hardship for many people in their 80s and 90s and for people who develop disabilities at relatively young ages."

How would a flat-rate COLA differ from current COLAs?

Currently, the Social Security Administration bases its COLA each year on average annual increases in the CPI-W, or the index for urban wage earners, from July through September. Every Social Security beneficiary's check is boosted by that COLA percentage.

In a flat-rate COLA, the percentage increase is calculated the same way, but it will only be applied to those in the 20th percentile. Whatever that dollar amount increase they receive, all Social Security recipients will receive the same that year, no matter what percentile they're in.

A flat-rate COLA set at the 20th percentile provides full benefits for two more years than what's currently predicted and is "highly progressive," the nonpartisan, nonprofit Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) said in an analysis .

articles.title: Social Security's coffers are so low even Republicans are talking about raising taxes — even if they 'get smeared'
articles.summary: With Social Security's trust fund set to run out in 2032 and benefits facing a 22% cut, some Republicans are now openly considering tax increases — including...
articles.body:
The trust fund underpinning Social Security's finances is scheduled to dry up in 2032, putting millions of retirees at risk of benefit cuts by the end of the next president's term. Some Republicans are starting to break with the party's longstanding opposition to tax increases to address the problem.

"We've got too many people who say, 'Well, we have to stay within the current income level or stay at the current tax rate,'" Rep. Tom Cole of Oklahoma, chair of the House Appropriations Committee, told the Washington Post in an interview. "I'm willing to look at the tax rate. I am willing to raise the amount of income through tax."

Such remarks from an influential Republican like Cole serve to deepen the GOP's willingness to at least entertain tax increases to extend the lifespan of a politically popular program like Social Security. In June, Social Security's trustees issued an annual report that said the program would be able to pay full benefits to retirees and disabled Americans until the fourth quarter of 2032, one quarter earlier than it had projected last year. At that point, the fund would be obligated to slash benefits by 22% to strengthen its financial footing.

Other Republicans are echoing Cole. "You'll probably have to do something on the payroll half of the money being paid into the system," Rep. Lloyd Smucker of Pennsylvania, who sits on the tax-writing House Ways and Means panel, recently told Roll Call.

Lifting the payroll tax cap gets a fresh look

In June, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio proposed wiping away the cap on Social Security payroll taxes, which are currently set at 12.4% and evenly divided between a worker and their employer. The payroll tax cap currently affects only the first $184,500 of wages and self-reported income, and that sum is annually indexed for inflation.

The pair called it a "no-brainer" solution to a vexing policy problem in a New York Times op-ed published June 23. "With rising prices and artificial intelligence causing economic uncertainty for the future, Social Security must remain a stable foundation to help retirees afford life's basic necessities," Warren and Moreno wrote.

articles.title: Social media account will live post 9/11 minute by minute
articles.summary: The account’s creator said he has prepared over 400 posts for the day.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — An account on social platform X is set to post live updates on Friday as if the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks were happening in real time — commemorating the 25th anniversary of the tragic events.

The account, 2001 Live , has been reposting news events from that year, illustrating how the time frame might have been viewed through the lens of current social media and is curated by Manny Marotta .

In a recent post, Marotta noted that there are currently 410 planned posts, which averages to a post every one to three minutes.

The posts will be posted manually, not automated, and will not include graphic images or video, according to the FAQ .

“I watched 240 hours of video footage, from news reporting to on-the-ground stringers to eyewitness testimony to academic documents, with the intent to form the most accurate-possible timeline of the event,” Marotta said in the post.

“I also had people professionally associated with and familiar with the event provide their own research, which was helpful,” he continued. “I did my very best to corroborate stories for accuracy and gather every possible detail of the day, and I hope that my work was adequate.”

It is not the only account on X dedicated to giving audiences a different perspective on historical events. One popular account, Real Time WWII , retweeted the events of the Second World War starting in 1941. It was run by an employee at the Museum of London.

As with the WWII account, Marotta’s project has spanned multiple years, beginning with his tweets about the events in 1997.

Although he is too young to remember 9/11 , Marotta said he is including it as part of his coverage of history. He also issued content guidelines around the topic.

“There was no conspiracy related to the September 11 attacks,” the X user wrote. “Those who seriously entertain conspiracy theories in the comments will be blocked.”

articles.body:
Qatar's budget deficit more than doubled to 21.2bn riyals (€5bn) in the second quarter of 2026, the Ministry of Finance announced on Tuesday.

The deficit stood at 10.3bn riyals (€2.44bn) in the first quarter.

Total revenue reached about 25.6bn riyals (€6.06bn), while expenditure amounted to approximately 46.9bn riyals (€11.1bn).

On 25 August, Qatari foreign ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari disputed reports about government spending cuts, saying figures had been taken out of context.

He said reported reductions of up to 30% applied only to operating expenses and excluded salaries and capital projects. He described the measures as temporary precautions introduced at the start of the regional crisis.

The two quarterly shortfalls bring the first-half deficit to 31.5bn riyals (€7.45bn), exceeding the 21.8bn riyal (€5.16bn) gap originally projected for the whole of 2026.

Disruption to Qatar's liquefied natural gas deliveries has also affected European buyers.

On 28 August, Italian utility company Edison said QatarEnergy had extended force majeure on deliveries into early November, bringing the number of affected LNG cargoes under their supply contract to 29.

Edison said it could obtain alternative gas supplies and continue meeting its commitments to customers.

Ship-tracking data reported on 7 September showed six empty Qatar-linked LNG carriers in the Gulf of Oman or heading towards it.

The report also cited Kpler data showing another empty vessel had crossed the Strait of Hormuz towards Qatar.

The same report said 15 loaded LNG carriers remained inside the Gulf, while two empty vessels had turned back after approaching the strait. These movements alone did not establish that regular exports had resumed.

articles.title: WHO report warns of link between smoking and infertility
articles.summary: A new report summarizes decades of evidence linking tobacco smoke with fertility problems.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Smoking at any point in your life could cause fertility issues , according to a new report from the World Health Organization (WHO).

The WHO’s Tobacco Free Initiative issued the report , summarizing research linking tobacco smoking and infertility, with the agency citing decades of evidence.

The organization defines infertility as failing to get pregnant after 12 or more months of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse, estimating that 1 in 6 people globally suffers from infertility.

Evidence cited in the report includes links between tobacco use and infertility in women and smoking being harmful to sperm quality and sexual function in men.

Secondhand smoke can also affect fertility, broadening the risk to those who are not smokers themselves, the researchers found.

WHO suggests that quitting smoking may help, with women who smoked in the past having a 25 percent lower risk of infertility than those who are active smokers.

The report also showed that men who smoke were more likely to have erectile dysfunction, problems with ejaculation and issues such as poor sperm motility, abnormal sperm shape and an absence of sperm in semen.

Research also showed that smoking reduced the success rate of fertility treatments .

The WHO said evidence on e-cigarettes , smokeless tobacco, waterpipes or hookahs and other emerging products still requires more research.

The report recommends that medical professionals educate people on the risks of smoking and provide resources to help people who want to quit.

Sept 9 (Reuters) - Mexico's annual inflation rate accelerated for the first time ‌in five months in August, official ‌data showed on Wednesday, backing up a cautious ​approach in the country's monetary policy.

Consumer prices in Latin America's second-largest economy rose 3.26% in the year through August, accelerating from ‌a 3.12% ⁠increase in July and but landing slightly below economists' forecasts in ⁠a Reuters poll that expected a 3.3% increase.

In June alone, consumer prices increased ​0.20%, following ​a 0.03% increase ​the prior month, ‌according to non-seasonally adjusted figures, and compared with economists' expectations of a 0.25% rise.

The closely watched core index, which strips out some volatile food and energy prices, ‌rose 0.16% during the ​month, below a 0.20% ​market forecasts ​and down slightly from the ‌0.23% recorded the previous ​month.

The annual ​core rate stood at 3.88%, also slowing from the 3.95% registered in July ​and below ‌expectations of a 3.93% increase.

(Reporting by ​Aida Pelaez-Fernandez and Ricardo Figueroa; ​Editing by Chizu Nomiyama )

articles.title: Oil rises past $100 a barrel after latest Middle East attacks
articles.summary: Oil prices climbed above $100 per barrel Wednesday for the first time since July as renewed fighting in the Middle East raised concerns about further disruptions to global energy supplies. Brent crude, the global benchmark, jumped nearly 3 percent to $100.72 per barrel in early trading, crossing $100 for the first time since late July. …
articles.body:
Oil prices climbed above $100 per barrel Wednesday for the first time since July as renewed fighting in the Middle East raised concerns about further disruptions to global energy supplies.

Brent crude , the global benchmark, jumped nearly 3 percent to $100.72 per barrel in early trading, crossing $100 for the first time since late July.

U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude rose 2.4 percent to $95.25 per barrel. The national average price of a gallon of gas also increased to $4.22 as of Wednesday morning, according to AAA .

The price of regular gas rose 7 cents overnight to more than $1 higher than its level a year ago. Diesel prices have also continued to rise after reaching a record high over the weekend, the numbers show.

The increase followed another round of attacks involving the U.S. and Iran. The U.S. military struck five Iranian oil tankers Tuesday, prompting Iran to say Wednesday that it attacked 10 vessels and a U.S. base in Jordan in retaliation.

Oil shipments from the region were already reduced significantly since the start of the war in late February. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz , a key shipping route through which about 20 percent of global energy supplies once passed through, has remained far below normal levels as the fighting continues.

Experts warned that the rising prices indicate growing market concerns over the vulnerability of oil exports and supply losses due to disruptions in the strait.

The rise in energy prices comes just weeks before the midterm elections, where Republicans seek to tighten their economic messaging to maintain their narrow majorities in the House and Senate. Gas prices above $4 per gallon have put additional focus on energy costs and inflation for voters heading into November.

“Oil investors are expressing their view about ​the impact of the latest bout of escalation in the Middle East in an unambiguous way,” PVM oil broker Tamas Varga told Reuters .

“They ⁠are voting with their dollar, and this vote strongly indicates that unless the Strait of Hormuz re-opens, and oil starts flowing again uninterruptedly, supply will not be aligned with demand ​in the foreseeable future,” Varga added.

articles.title: Group of bipartisan lawmakers ask US government to ban several hack-for-hire firms | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The three Indian companies are accused of using hackers to steal information used to sway litigation.
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers has asked the U.S. government to ban several hack-for-hire firms — companies that carry out cyberattacks on behalf of paying clients. The lawmakers accuse the firms of targeting Americans and abusing foreign courts to silence U.S. reporting on their activities.

Democratic senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, and Republican congressman Pat Harrigan, on Wednesday sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, urging him to add three Indian companies to the department’s economic sanctions “ entity list .”

The list effectively bars U.S. businesses from transacting with a named entity, with the aim of restricting the companies from accessing critical technology needed to function, including software licenses and cloud infrastructure.

In the letter sent to Lutnick and shared with TechCrunch, the lawmakers say BellTroX, CyberRoot, and Sunkissed Organic Farms (which previously operated under its former name, Appin) have for more than a decade conducted cyberattacks and targeted espionage against Americans, business owners, and their lawyers, to “manipulate ongoing litigation.”

The lawmakers say that these mercenary hacking companies have stolen data from thousands of Americans, and accuse the hackers of an “aggressive censorship campaign” to suppress public awareness of their alleged activities.

“This coordinated effort effectively allows foreign entities to use foreign courts to keep the American public in the dark about cyber threats to their own country and undermines the fundamental constitutional rights of U.S. citizens,” the lawmakers said.

It’s not clear if the Commerce Department will add the companies to its entity list, and a spokesperson did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

The letter’s request to add the companies to the entity list follows extensive reporting and media investigations on the hack-for-hire industry, documenting how hackers are paid to break into the inboxes and devices of executives, lawmakers, and military officials to gain an advantage in lawsuits or influence their outcomes.

One of the companies, Appin, previously secured a global court order from an Indian court forcing Reuters to take down its reporting on the company while Reuters appealed the order. The notice that appeared on the page at the time said that Reuters “stands by its reporting.” The order was later lifted and the report republished.

The digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation previously defended two news organizations, Techdirt and the MuckRock Foundation, from legal threats after Appin engaged in “a campaign of bullying and censorship seeking to wipe out stories” about the company’s involvement in mercenary hacking.

The lawmakers’ letter said that the hack-for-hire companies “operated at the behest of the Qatari government” and that their targets included a former senior Republican lawmaker.

Appin has been linked to Qatar before. Earlier reporting tied Appin to a campaign of cyberattacks against FIFA officials, reportedly directed by Qatar as part of an effort to protect its plans to host the 2022 World Cup.

A representative from the Qatari government in Washington, D.C. did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

An email from TechCrunch to Anuj Khare, a director at Sunkissed Organic Farms, went unreturned.

Separate reporting by The New Yorker and digital investigative unit The Citizen Lab has also documented espionage activity by the two other hack-for-hire firms named in the lawmakers’ letter, BellTroX and CyberRoot.

TechCrunch sought comment from representatives at CyberRoot, but did not hear back prior to publication. BellTroX could not be reached for comment.

articles.title: NCAA says it can’t overturn last-second Michigan win
articles.summary: The NCAA says it cannot overturn the result of Saturday’s Western Michigan vs. Michigan football game, which ended in controversy after officials put a second back on the clock, allowing the Wolverines to score a game-winning touchdown. Earlier this week, Mid-American Conference Commissioner Jon Steinbrecher asked the NCAA to declare Western Michigan, one of its…
articles.body:
The NCAA says it cannot overturn the result of Saturday’s Western Michigan vs. Michigan football game, which ended in controversy after officials put a second back on the clock, allowing the Wolverines to score a game-winning touchdown.

Earlier this week, Mid-American Conference Commissioner Jon Steinbrecher asked the NCAA to declare Western Michigan, one of its member schools, “as the actual winner of the game for purposes of their respective rankings, evaluations and selection deliberations, and take such other corrective action as may be within their authority.”

Steinbrecher’s request followed a controversial ending to Saturday’s game in Ann Arbor.

The Big Ten officiating crew that night determined a Western Michigan defensive player touched the ball while out of bounds on a last-second Hail Mary by the Wolverines.

After the officials put a second back on the clock, Michigan pulled off an improbable touchdown to win the game, 13-12.

Steinbrecher argued “replay protocol was not properly followed in determining whether time remained on the game clock.”

The NCAA, in a statement to The Hill, said its “football playing rules do not have a protocol for overturning the outcome of a game.”

“No rule decision may be changed after the ball is next legally snapped, legally free-kicked or the second or fourth periods have ended,” the NCAA rules state, with the association noting “the Division I Football Bowl Subdivision Oversight Committee also does not have the authority to overturn the outcome of a game.”

Michigan, which opened the season ranked 16th in the AP Top 25 poll, dropped out of the poll following the victory and faces a major test against No. 11 Oklahoma this weekend.

articles.title: Microsoft, AFT unveil AI safety and privacy standard for schools
articles.summary: Microsoft and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) unveiled a new AI safety and privacy standard for schools Wednesday, after two of the nation’s largest school districts placed strict new limits on AI use. The national standard bars student and educator data from being used to train AI models and from being sold or used…
articles.body:
Microsoft and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) unveiled a new AI safety and privacy standard for schools Wednesday, after two of the nation’s largest school districts placed strict new limits on AI use.

The national standard bars student and educator data from being used to train AI models and from being sold or used for advertising. It also requires human oversight of AI models, in addition to ensuring families receive “clear, plain-language guides” about the technology and its safeguards.

Microsoft plans to make the protections available for school districts to add to new or existing contracts starting in November.

“We have forged a hard-fought, iron-clad privacy agreement with real teeth that protects students and families, because no one else, including the federal government, has stepped up to do the real work,” AFT President Randi Weingarten said in a statement.

“We can get angrier and angrier, or we can act decisively; anything less than legally enforceable provisions is simply a wish list,” she continued.

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith touted the protections for setting a “high bar for child privacy and AI safety,” underscoring that they will be available to every school district across the country.

The agreement comes after both New York City and Los Angeles public schools announced new restrictions on AI for the academic year.

New York City schools banned student-facing AI through eighth grade, with high school students allowed to use prevetted programs. Individual screen time is also limited to students in third grade and above, with guidance to cap one-on-one screen time to 30 to 45 minutes a day up through eighth grade.

The Los Angeles Unified School District also blocked access to generative AI on district devices for all students, according to the Los Angeles Times.

articles.title: Anthropic researchers warn out-of-control AI could destroy humans
articles.summary: Several current and former Anthropic researchers are offering a stark warning about AI, suggesting the technology they are developing could destroy humanity in the near future. Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both Anthropic and OpenAI, argued Tuesday that neither company is acting responsibly as they race toward superintelligence and accused the AI firms of…
articles.body:
Several current and former Anthropic researchers are offering a stark warning about AI, suggesting the technology they are developing could destroy humanity in the near future.

Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both Anthropic and OpenAI, argued Tuesday that neither company is acting responsibly as they race toward superintelligence and accused the AI firms of “gambling with our lives.”

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote in a post on the social platform X, after announcing he had resigned from Anthropic.

“This is not a marketing stunt,” he continued. “If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.”

His comments were quickly echoed by other Anthropic researchers.

Evan Hubinger, who currently heads up alignment science at Anthropic, said “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans ,” adding he thinks there is a greater than 10 percent chance this occurs within the next decade.

He suggested Anthropic is “trying its best” but underscored that researchers don’t have a plan to keep superintelligence aligned with their interests.

Samuel Marks, who leads scalable oversight at the company, similarly said AI developers believe their technology could cause “human extinction” or other bad outcomes in the next few years.

“Why do AI developers continue despite the risk?” he wrote in a post on X . “Due to a mixture of commercial incentives and a belief that they are in a race with other, less responsible AI developers that will abuse the technology or develop it less safely.”

“I work on safety research at Anthropic because I hope my work will reduce the chance of these extinction-level bad outcomes,” Marks added.

It is the latest warning from AI researchers about the risks underlying the increasingly powerful technology they are building.

More than 1,300 employees at frontier AI companies signed on to an open letter in July urging the U.S. government to support an international effort to pace automated AI development.

This effort was ultimately backed by both Anthropic and OpenAI. However, the two companies are also racing one another and fellow AI firms to develop the technology and secure funding, including by going public.

Despite this dynamic, Coxon suggested Tuesday he is “optimistic about the potential for coordination” following “warning shots” from recent incidents in which rogue AI agents gained access to the internet and independently hacked into other companies.

articles.title: Trump administration names permanent FDA division leaders
articles.summary: The Trump administration permanently filled four key leadership roles in the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Tuesday, the agency announced, following the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA. The acting leaders in charge of regulating drugs, vaccines and tobacco will transition into the jobs permanently. Michael Davis, a psychiatrist, will be director…
articles.body:
The Trump administration permanently filled four key leadership roles in the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Tuesday, the agency announced, following the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA.

The acting leaders in charge of regulating drugs, vaccines and tobacco will transition into the jobs permanently.

Michael Davis, a psychiatrist, will be director of the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research; former Merck official Karim Mikhail will be the permanent director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research; and Bret Koplow, an attorney who has been at the FDA since 2011, will become director of the Center for Tobacco Products.

Jared Seehafer will be the FDA’s first deputy commissioner for technology and artificial intelligence. Seehafer, an entrepreneur and executive who founded a life science software company, first joined the FDA in 2025 as an adviser.

The newly created position underscores the administration’s commitment to accelerating AI innovation and ensuring an effective regulatory framework for emerging technologies, the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement.

The moves will bring continuity to FDA leadership that has been roiled by frequent turnover and leadership departures, including President Trump’s first FDA commissioner of his second term, Marty Makary, who resigned in May.

If confirmed, Overton would take charge of an agency that’s viewed as less trustworthy and more politicized than it has been in any previous administration. Commissioners and center directors are typically not involved in day-to-day drug approvals.

Makary’s tenure atop the agency was marred by clashes with staff, politicized review decisions, and disagreements with the biotechnology industry. Since his departure, the FDA has been led in an acting capacity by Kyle Diamantas.

Mikhail has drawn praise from industry groups, which call him a stabilizing force.

During the tenure of his predecessor, Vinay Prasad, hundreds of workers left the agency’s biologics division and morale slumped. Prasad also rejected at least five drugs that advocates and the FDA itself previously considered promising.

“These selections are not just about filling leadership roles — they signal the direction we are heading,” Diamantas said in a statement.

He said the new leaders will help the FDA “attract and retain best-in-class talent” while helping it build a workforce that will accelerate innovation across the FDA centers.

articles.title: Bipartisan coalition pushes Trump administration on AI security framework release
articles.summary: A group of organizations from both sides of the aisle called on President Trump to publicly release his administration’s framework on government AI testing, arguing the closed-door policy raises concerns around transparency. “The government has a fundamental responsibility to share the parameters of the process for reviewing frontier AI models prior to wider deployment,” the…
articles.body:
A group of organizations from both sides of the aisle called on President Trump to publicly release his administration’s framework on government AI testing, arguing the closed-door policy raises concerns around transparency.

“The government has a fundamental responsibility to share the parameters of the process for reviewing frontier AI models prior to wider deployment,” the organizations wrote in the Wednesday letter . “Through this framework, the federal government will obtain initial access and visibility into the most transformative technologies we have ever seen.”

The letter, first reported by Semafor , was led by the Center for Democracy and Technology and Americans for Responsible Innovation, a nonprofit pushing for tighter guardrails on AI development.

The technology community was thrown off guard last month after the White House completed but decided not to release a long-awaited framework for how the government plans to test the security of private AI models ahead of their release.

The framework was a required part of Trump’s June executive order, which officially launched a new process for AI companies to voluntarily share their models with the government for up to 30 days before releasing them publicly.

While the order gave multiple agencies 60 days to develop a classified benchmarking process that would stay behind closed doors, it also called for a framework on how a company can be designated a “covered frontier model” and collaborate with the federal government to select “trusted partners” that also have early access to new models.

Among the signatories are the left-of-center consumer rights group Public Citizen, the Tech Oversight Project and conservative-leaning groups like the R Street Institute and Americans for Prosperity.

The organizations argued that while there may be legitimate reasons to withhold some portions for confidentiality or national security purposes, “the government has an unequivocal duty to disclose information about the framework’s standards, requirements, structure, and operational details.”

The letter warned this could decrease public trust in the government’s oversight of advanced AI, while disadvantaging smaller firms.

Representatives from Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, Microsoft, Nvidia and some other smaller companies attended a briefing from the White House on the framework, but other parts of the AI industry were not looped in.

Several groups have pushed back against the White House’s decision in recent weeks. The nonprofit organization Protect Democracy sued the Trump administration earlier this month to enforce a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request asking for information about the framework.

The Foundation for American Innovation, a center-right think tank focused on technology and policy, also filed a FOIA request to the White House’s Office of the National Cyber Director for the release of the framework last month.

The framework comes at a time of intense scrutiny about the security of AI models and the role governments should play in their release.

OpenAI in July revealed its agents hacked into the systems of open-source tech firm Hugging Face, sending shock waves through the industry.

Anthropic and Meta later disclosed other incidents in which a misconfiguration by the cybersecurity company Irregular allowed models in isolated environments to access the internet and hack other systems.
